about.title: Nevada City Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Nevada City's mix of small businesses, contractors, and rural work sites near SR-49 and SR-20 means workplace injuries here often involve more than one responsible party. While California generally requires injured workers to go through workers' compensation rather than sue their employer directly, that system doesn't cover everything—and it doesn't apply to negligent third parties like equipment manufacturers, subcontractors, or property owners who weren't your direct employer. If a defective tool, an unsafe job site controlled by someone else, or a careless driver caused your injury on the job, you may have a separate legal path worth exploring. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your case directly—we simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney in our network who can look at what happened and explain your options clearly, without pressure or upfront cost.

whyChoose.title: Why Nevada City Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: We Understand the Third-Party Distinction
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but if a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible. We help you get matched with someone who can sort out which path applies.

items.title: We Know the Clock Is Running
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and any third-party claim carries a 2-year deadline under California law. Waiting too long can limit your options, so we help you move quickly toward the right attorney.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal—We Won't Let That Scare You Off
items.desc: California law protects workers from retaliation for reporting an injury or pursuing a claim. If you're worried about your job, an independent attorney in our network can explain your protections plainly.

items.question: I was hurt working near SR-20 outside Nevada City—can I still file a claim?
items.answer: Yes. Location doesn't change your right to report a workplace injury or explore a third-party claim if someone other than your employer contributed to what happened. We can connect you with an attorney who will look at the specifics of where and how the injury occurred.

items.question: Does workers' comp mean I can't sue anyone?
items.answer: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, so you typically can't sue them directly even if they were careless. However, a negligent third party—like a subcontractor, driver, or equipment manufacturer—can still be held separately liable, and that claim follows a 2-year deadline.

items.question: What if my employer discourages me from reporting my injury?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal in California, regardless of how small your employer is or where you work in Nevada County. You still have 30 days to report the injury, and an independent attorney can advise you on documenting what happened and protecting yourself.
